pages.title: How to Quote a Job: Steps and a Worked Example
pages.desc: How to quote a job from first call to finished quote: what to ask, how to price it, what to write down, and a garden fence example you can edit.
pages.h1: How to quote a job, from first call to finished quote
pages.lead: Here is how to quote a job in the right order, from the first phone call to a quote the customer can accept. One garden fence job runs through every step.
pages.answer: To quote a job, first find out exactly what the customer wants. Price the materials, your time, your overheads and your profit. Write one clear quote and send it the same day or the next morning. The quote needs a short scope, a total, what is not included, payment terms and a valid-until date. The finished example below loads into the quote maker, so you can change it.

A worked example from first call to finished quote
Write the quote so it can be accepted
pages.content:
Get the details before you price anything

Do the asking before the pricing. A price built on a guess ends up too low for you or too high for the customer.

On the first call, ask these questions and write down the answers.

  • What do you want done, in your own words?
  • Where is the job, and how easy is it to reach with tools and materials?
  • What is there now, and does all of it come out?
  • Does the work need a permit, or anyone's permission, such as a landlord or a neighbour?
  • Is anything still undecided, like colours, styles or finishes?
  • Is there a date you must hit, or a budget in mind?
  • Who decides, and who pays?
  • When can I come and look?

At the visit, measure everything and take photos of what is there. Look for anything that could cost extra, such as poor access, hard ground or old work that hides a problem. If you cannot visit, ask for photos and measurements, and give an estimate until you have seen the job.

Then write the job in your own words and send it to the customer to confirm. Two or three lines are enough: what you will do and what you will not do. A misunderstanding caught now costs one message. Caught halfway through the job, it costs days.

Decide between a fixed quote and an estimate

In plain terms, a quote is a firm price and an estimate is your best guess. Rules for each differ from place to place, so check the ones where you work.

  • Give a fixed quote when you can see and measure the whole job. The customer gets one price, and you carry the risk if the work takes longer.
  • Give an estimate when you cannot know the size of the job until you start, as with fault-finding or repairs behind a wall. Say what could move the price.
  • Use a provisional sum when only one part of the job is unknown. Give it its own line, say what it covers, and settle it at the real cost once you know.
  • Offer options when the customer has not chosen between two ways of doing something. Price each option on its own line.

Whichever you choose, say so on the document. Put the word Quotation or Estimate at the top, and list anything that could change the price. A customer who was told the price could move is easier to deal with when it does.

Price the job in four parts

Every job price has four parts. Work out each one, then add them up.

  • Materials: everything you need, at today's supplier prices, plus waste and delivery.
  • Labour: the hours the job takes at your hourly rate, including travel, setting up and clearing up.
  • Overheads: the cost of running your business that no customer pays for directly, such as your van, tools and insurance.
  • Profit: what is left for you once every cost is paid.

The sums are in our guide to pricing a job quote, which has a calculator. Work out your price there, then come back to write the quote.

The customer does not need to see your overheads or your profit. They can sit inside your rates, so the quote shows clear lines and still covers your costs.

A worked example from first call to finished quote

The job: replace 12 m (40 ft) of rotten garden fence with new panels on new posts. Here is how to make a quote for it, step by step.

  1. First call. The customer says the old fence is falling down and wants the same height. You ask the questions above. You learn that the fence is theirs, that the side gate stays, and that they want the work done before December.
  2. Site visit. You measure 12 m along the boundary and work out that the new fence needs 7 panels, each 1.83 m (6 ft) wide, and 8 posts. Six panels fall short, so the seventh is cut to fit. The ground is firm, but two old posts look as if they are set in concrete. You take photos of everything.
  3. Scope. You write two lines: take down and remove 12 m of old fence, then set 8 new posts and hang 7 panels, 1.8 m (6 ft) high. The customer replies to confirm.
  4. Fixed price or estimate. Everything is clear except those old post bases. You give a fixed quote, with a provisional sum on its own line for extra digging.
  5. Price. You work out materials, labour, overheads and profit, then turn the result into a few clear lines.
  6. Write and send. You number the quote, date it, add a valid-until date, a deposit and how to accept, then email the PDF the next morning.

This is the finished quote. The prices are examples to replace with your own.

QUOTATION Q-104222 October 2026, valid until 21 November 2026

Replace 12 m of garden fence at the back of the house: 7 new panels on 8 new posts, and the old fence taken away.

DescriptionQtyRateAmount
Fence panels, 1.8 m (6 ft) high, treated timber7£42.00£294.00
Posts, 2.4 m (8 ft), with concrete mix8£28.00£224.00
Screws, brackets and fixings1£35.00£35.00
Delivery of materials1£40.00£40.00
Take down the old fence and take it away1£150.00£150.00
Labour to set the posts and hang the panels (two people, per day)2£380.00£760.00
Provisional sum: extra digging if old post bases are set in concrete1£120.00£120.00
Subtotal£1,623.00
VAT 20%£324.60
Total including VAT£1,947.60

Not included: painting or staining, replacing the gate, and moving plants.

Provisional sum: the total includes an allowance for extra digging. The final bill uses the real cost, up or down.

Payment: 30% deposit (£584.28 including VAT) by bank transfer to book the dates. The balance of £1,363.32 is due when the fence is finished, adjusted for the provisional sum.

Changes: any extra work is priced and agreed with you in writing before we do it.

To accept, reply 'accepted' to the email this quote came with.

Each line tells the customer something.

  • Panels and posts: the customer can see what they are buying and count it when it arrives.
  • Fixings and delivery: small costs are listed, so none of them turns up later as a surprise.
  • Taking down the old fence: the customer knows you will take it away.
  • Labour: two people for two days shows how long you expect to be there.
  • Provisional sum: an allowance for the one thing you cannot see. It is in the total, and the notes say it is settled at the real cost.
  • VAT and total: tax sits on its own line, so the customer sees the price before and after it.

Press Load this example into the quote maker under the quote. It opens in the quote maker on this page, where you can change any line and download the PDF. The quote maker is free and needs no signup. You choose the currency and type your own tax rate, so a US job can use dollars and your local sales tax. The notes are plain text, so the tool does not recalculate them. If you change a line, the currency or the tax, work out the deposit and the balance again and change them in the notes, along with the tax wording.

Write the quote so it can be accepted

A quote the customer can say yes to leaves nothing for them to ask. Put all of this on the page.

  • A quote number, the date and a valid-until date.
  • Your details, the customer's details and the address of the job.
  • One line on the scope, then itemised lines with a quantity, a rate and an amount.
  • Tax on its own line if you charge it, then the total.
  • What is not included, naming anything the customer might assume is in the price.
  • Payment terms: the deposit, when the balance is due and how to pay.
  • How changes are handled: extra work is priced and agreed before you do it.
  • How to accept, in one clear step.

Wording you can copy for each part is in our guide on how to write a professional quote. For the acceptance step, see our quote acceptance wording.

Choose the valid-until date with care. It should give the customer time to decide, and it should end before a rise in your material prices can hurt you. Ask for a deposit when you must buy materials or book dates, and write the amount on the quote.

Send it and follow up

Send the quote the same day, or the next morning at the latest, while the job is fresh in the customer's mind. Download it as a PDF and attach it to your own email, because QuotationMaker does not send emails.

Keep the email short. Give the total, and say whether it includes VAT or tax. Add the valid-until date and how to accept. Email wording you can copy is in our guide on sending a quote to a client.

If you hear nothing, send a short, polite message a few days later, and another before the valid-until date. After that, let the quote lapse.

If the job changes before the customer accepts, send a revised quotation with a new date that says what changed. When the customer says yes, send a quotation confirmation with the start date, so you both have the same plan.

A logo helps the customer recognise your business. The free PDF has a small 'Made with GetQuotationMaker.com' line at the bottom of each page. Pro costs $9, paid once, and removes that line and adds your logo.

Checklist before you press send

Read the quote once as the customer would, then check each of these.

  • The customer's name and the job address are right.
  • The customer has confirmed the scope in writing.
  • The scope says what you will do, in plain words.
  • Every line has a quantity, a rate and an amount, and the amounts add up.
  • Tax is shown on its own line, or the quote says none is charged.
  • Anything the customer might assume is included, but is not, is listed as not included.
  • Any unknown part has its own labelled line or a note.
  • The deposit, the balance and how to pay are written out.
  • The deposit and the balance in the notes match the total.
  • The quote has a number, today's date and a valid-until date.
  • It says how to accept.
  • Your phone number and email are on it, so the customer can ask a question.
  • You have noted a date to follow up if you hear nothing.

faq.q: What is the difference between a quote and an estimate?
faq.a: A quote is a firm price for a defined job. An estimate is your best guess and can change. Say which one you are giving at the top of the document, and check the rules where you work, because they differ from place to place.

faq.q: How long should a quote be valid for?
faq.a: Long enough for the customer to decide, and short enough that a rise in material prices cannot hurt you. The example on this page uses 30 days. Use less time if your supplier's prices change often.

faq.q: Do I show my profit and overheads on the quote?
faq.a: You do not have to. They can sit inside your rates and totals. Show lines the customer can check: materials with quantities, labour as days or hours, and any allowance on its own line.

faq.q: How do I quote a job I cannot see?
faq.a: Ask the customer for photos and measurements, and give an estimate instead of a fixed quote. Say what you based it on, and offer to confirm the price after a visit.

faq.q: What if the work changes after the customer says yes?
faq.a: Tell the customer before you do any extra work, and agree the new price in writing before you start it.

faq.q: Do I need to sign up to make the quote?
faq.a: No. The quote maker is free and has no account. Your business name, email and address are remembered on your own device, so the next quote is faster. It does not send emails, so attach the PDF to your own message.

pages.h1: Quotation terms and conditions: wording to copy
pages.lead: These quotation terms and conditions are short blocks for the notes of a quote: how long the price holds, the deposit, what is left out, changes and cancellation. Each block says when to use it.
pages.answer: Quotation terms and conditions are the short notes at the bottom of a quote. They tell the client how long the price holds, what they pay and when, what is left out, what happens if the job changes and what happens if they cancel. Copy the blocks on this page, replace the highlighted placeholders with your own details and paste them into the notes box of your quote. A large or risky job needs a written contract instead.

A finished quote with terms in the notes box
pages.content:
What to put in the terms of a quote

Terms on a quote should be short. The client reads them before saying yes, so they only need to cover what the client must know to decide. Five clauses answer the questions a client has at that point: valid until, deposit and payment, exclusions, changes and cancellation.

Each section below has wording you can copy, with a note on when to use it. Think of the blocks as a quote terms and conditions template: copy what fits and delete the rest. Square brackets mark the parts you change. Put the finished clauses in the notes box under the line items of your quote. The price and the line items come first, and our guides on how to quote a job and how to write a professional quote cover them.

These notes state your offer clearly. They do not replace a contract. A cap on liability, indemnity, ownership of designs, governing law and late-payment interest all belong in a written contract, and a lawyer is the right person to draft one. Use the blocks here for the notes of a one-page quote, and ask for a contract when the job is large or risky.

Valid until: how long the price stays open

The quote validity period is how long your price stays on offer. After the expiry date the price can change. Give the expiry as a date, such as 20 November 2026. Zigaflow gives the reason: a number of days leaves it open when the count starts, at issue, on receipt or on the day the email was opened. A client and a trader who read it differently tend to find out after prices have moved.

For how long, ShiftFlow suggests starting with 14 to 30 days. For prices or schedules that move fast, it puts the figure at 7 to 14 days. It describes the range as a business decision, and no law or industry standard fixes it. Zigaflow adds that when you sell to another business, no law sets a default period, so your quote decides it.

Valid until

Use on most quotes. Change the date, and keep it as a calendar date.

This quote is valid until [date]. After that date the price may change. If you accept later, we will recheck the price and confirm it in writing first.

Valid until, when material prices move

Use when the price depends on supplier costs that change often. Pick a shorter date.

Material prices change often. This quote is valid until [date]. After that date we will recheck the cost of materials before we confirm the price.

An expiry date on its own does not hold a start date for the client. ShiftFlow says the date only shows when you will look at your price and availability again. If you want to hold dates for the client, tie them to a step such as the deposit, and say so in the deposit wording below.

If the date passes and the client then says yes, treat the old quote as closed. Recheck your costs and your availability, then send a revised quotation with a new date.

Sources checked 30 October 2026: ShiftFlow: How long should a contractor quote be valid?; Zigaflow: Quotation validity.

Deposit and payment terms

Say how much you ask for up front, when the rest is due and how to pay. Write the deposit as an amount, so the client sees the sum they will transfer. Work it out from your own costs: it should cover the materials you must buy and the dates you hold.

Deposit and balance

Use on short jobs where you buy materials or book dates. Change both amounts so they add up to the total.

Deposit: [deposit amount] is due when you accept this quote. It books [start date] and pays for the materials we order.

The balance of [balance amount] is due [when, for example on completion].

On a longer job, split the price into stages. Tie each stage to something the client can see, such as the delivery of materials or the end of the first week.

Payment in stages

Use on jobs that run for weeks. Name each stage by something the client can check.

Payment is in [number] stages.

[Amount] is due when you accept this quote. [Amount] is due when [stage, for example the materials are delivered]. The balance of [amount] is due when the job is finished.

Payment due date and method

Put this after the deposit wording. Keep your bank details on the invoice.

Invoices are due [number] days after the invoice date. Pay by [method, for example bank transfer] and use the invoice number as the reference.

Once the client says yes, send a quotation confirmation that repeats the total, the deposit and the start date.

Exclusions and assumptions

A client sees one total and reads it as the whole job. Tell them what is not in it. Name the things they might expect to find in the price, and add one sentence that closes the gap: anything not listed is not included.

Exclusions

List what a client might assume is included. Delete the items that do not apply to this job.

Not included: [item], [item].

Anything not listed in this quote is not included in the price.

Then list what the price assumes. These are the conditions that must be true for your price to hold: access to the work area, working hours, materials the client supplies and the state of the existing work.

Assumptions

Use when the price depends on conditions you do not control. Keep only the lines that are true for this job.

The price assumes the following.

Access: we can reach the work area from [start time] to [finish time] on [days].
Materials: you supply [item] and have it on site by [date].
Existing work: the [wall, floor or pipework] is sound and needs no repair.
Services: power and water are on and free to use.

Changes to the job

Jobs change after the quote goes out. The client adds a socket or picks a dearer tile. You open a wall and find a problem. Write down in advance how this is handled: extra work is priced and agreed before it is done, and the total changes by the agreed amount.

Changes and extra work

Use on every quote. It covers changes the client asks for.

Changes: any extra work, or a change to the quantity or the specification above, is priced and agreed with you in writing before we do it. The total changes by the agreed amount.

Problems found during the work

Use on repairs, renovations and any job where part of the work is hidden. Change the examples to fit your trade.

Hidden problems: if we find a problem that could not be seen when we quoted, such as [rot, damp or old wiring], we will stop that part of the work and tell you. We will send a price for the extra work and carry on once you agree.

If the job changes before the client accepts, send a revised quotation that shows the new price and says what changed. After they accept, put the extra work in a short email and wait for a written yes before you start it.

Cancellation

Keep the cancellation clause short. Say what happens if the client cancels before the start date, and what happens once you have ordered materials or spent time on the job. Cancelling is the reverse of accepting, so keep the two clauses side by side. Wording for the acceptance side is in our quote acceptance wording.

One more thing matters when the client is a person buying work for their home. Citizens Advice tells customers in England that they have a 14-day cooling-off period to cancel building or decorating work they arranged by phone, online or away from the trader's premises, such as at their home. Inside those 14 days, the customer can cancel and get all their money back if the business has not started the work. The period starts the day after the customer gives the go-ahead. The page calls 14 days the absolute minimum a seller must give. It lists exceptions, such as specially made items, and urgent repairs or maintenance the customer asks for.

If the customer asks for the work to start inside that period, and the business has given the cancellation details, the customer pays a part of the agreed price for the work done. If the work starts without the customer asking for it, the customer can cancel and get a full refund. The business must give the customer details of how to cancel. If it does not, the cooling-off period is extended by 14 days from the date the customer receives them, up to a maximum of 1 year. Rules differ in other places, so check the ones where you work.

So give a home customer in England written details of how to cancel, with the quote. This covers a customer who agreed the work by phone, online or at their home. The page does not mention emailed quotes, so if the client accepts by replying to your email, treat that as agreeing online and give them the details too. Let your own cancellation charges apply only after the 14 days. Materials you order inside the 14 days are at your own risk. Even if the customer asked you to start sooner, they pay only for the part of the job completed when they cancel. The line 'This does not affect your legal rights' is a reminder. It does not replace those details.

Cooling-off period (home customers)

Use when the client is a home customer in England who agreed the work by phone, online or at their home. Send it with the quote and add your contact details. It follows the rule as Citizens Advice describes it for England, so check the rules where you work.

Cooling-off period: you have 14 days to cancel this work, starting the day after you give the go-ahead. If you cancel in that time and we have not started the work, you get all your money back.

If you ask us to start the work inside the 14 days and then cancel, you pay a part of the agreed price for the work done by then.

To cancel, contact us at [your contact details].

Cancelling before the work starts

Use on every job with a start date. The charges apply as written to business clients. For a home customer in England who agreed the work by phone, online or at their home, they apply only after the cooling-off period above. Fill in your hourly rate, or delete that sentence. The last sentence stays.

Cancellation: you can cancel this quote at any time before work starts by telling us in writing. If we have already ordered materials for you that we cannot return, you pay for them. If we have spent time on your job, you pay for that time at [hourly rate]. We refund the rest of your deposit. This does not affect your legal rights.

Sources checked 30 October 2026: Citizens Advice: Cancelling building or decorating work.

A finished quote with terms in the notes box

The job: strip the old tiles from the walls of a small bathroom, prepare the walls and tile about 8 m² of wall. The client is a home customer in England who accepts by replying to the email. The quote below holds all five clauses in its notes, with the cooling-off wording added. The prices are example prices to replace with your own.

QUOTATION Q-106830 October 2026, valid until 20 November 2026

Strip the old wall tiles in a small bathroom, prepare the walls and tile about 8 m² of wall with new porcelain tiles.

DescriptionQtyRateAmount
Strip old wall tiles and take away the waste1£180.00£180.00
Prepare walls: patch, level and prime1£95.00£95.00
Porcelain wall tiles, per m², including waste (tile allowance)9£36.00£324.00
Tile adhesive, grout and sealant1£72.00£72.00
Delivery of materials1£35.00£35.00
Labour to tile the walls (one tiler, per day)3£185.00£555.00
Subtotal£1,261.00
VAT 20%£252.20
Total including VAT£1,513.20

Valid until the date shown at the top of this quote. After that date the price may change, and we will recheck it before you accept.

Not included: new bathroom fittings, floor tiling, plumbing or electrical work, and painting the ceiling. Anything not listed in this quote is not included in the price.

The price assumes: access from 8:00 to 17:00 on weekdays, power and water on, and walls that need only light patching. The tile allowance is £36 per m², so dearer tiles change the price.

Payment: a deposit of £520.00 including VAT is due when you accept. It books the start date and pays for the materials. The balance of £993.20 is due within 7 days of our invoice, which we send when the job is finished. Pay by bank transfer.

Changes: extra work, or a change to the tiles or the area, is priced and agreed with you in writing before we do it. If we find a hidden problem behind the old tiles, we will stop that part of the work, tell you and send a price for the repair.

Cooling-off period: you have 14 days to cancel this work, starting the day after you give the go-ahead. If you cancel in that time and we have not started the work, you get all your money back. If you ask us to start the work inside the 14 days and then cancel, you pay a part of the agreed price for the work done by then. To cancel, email us at the address on this quote.

Cancellation: after the cooling-off period, you can cancel before work starts by telling us in writing. If we have ordered materials we cannot return, you pay for them. If we have spent time on your job, you pay for that time at £23 an hour. We refund the rest of your deposit. This does not affect your legal rights.

Prices exclude VAT. VAT at 20% is shown in the totals above and the total includes VAT.

To accept, reply 'accepted' to the email this quote came with.

Here is where each clause sits.

  • Valid until: the notes point to the calendar date at the top of the quote, so there is one date and no count of days.
  • Exclusions and assumptions: the notes list what is left out and the conditions behind the price. The tile allowance is stated per m², so a dearer tile changes the price in a way the client can see.
  • Payment: the deposit and the balance are amounts, and they add up to the total of £1,513.20. The deposit is enough to cover the materials in the quote, VAT included.
  • Changes: extra work is agreed in writing first, and a hidden problem behind the old tiles has its own sentence.
  • Cancellation: the client gets all their money back if they cancel inside the 14-day cooling-off period before work starts. After that, they pay only for materials you cannot return and for time already spent.

You choose the currency and type your own tax rate and tax label, so the example works for a job in dollars with sales tax too. The notes are plain text, so the tool does not recalculate them. If you change a line, the currency or the tax, work out the deposit and the balance again and update the notes. The validity line points to the valid-until date at the top of the quote. If you also type a date into the notes, check that the two match. The cancellation line points to the email address on your quote, so type your email into the form before you download.

Checklist before you send

Read the quote once as the client would, then check each of these.

  • The quote has a number and today's date.
  • The valid-until date is a calendar date, not a number of days.
  • The total is stated, and the quote says whether tax is included.
  • The deposit and the balance are written as amounts that add up to the total.
  • Exclusions and assumptions are listed.
  • Changes, extra work and cancellation each have a sentence, and home customers in England get the cooling-off wording.
  • The quote says how to accept, in one step.
  • Your phone number and email are on it.
  • The PDF opens and reads well.

Send the quote with a short email. Our guide to sending a quote to a client has wording for it.

The quote maker is free and needs no signup. A free PDF has a small 'Made with GetQuotationMaker.com' line at the bottom of each page. Pro costs $9, paid once, and removes that line, adds your logo and turns any quote into an invoice PDF.

faq.q: What should the terms on a quote cover?
faq.a: Five things: how long the price holds, the deposit and when you are paid, what is not included, how changes are handled and what happens if the client cancels. Keep each one to a few sentences.

faq.q: How long should a quote be valid?
faq.a: ShiftFlow suggests starting with 14 to 30 days, and 7 to 14 days for prices or schedules that move fast. It describes the length as a business decision, and no law or industry standard fixes it. Give the expiry as a calendar date.

faq.q: What do I do when a quote has expired?
faq.a: Treat the old quote as closed. Recheck your costs and your availability, then send a revised quotation with a new date.

faq.a: No. On its own the date only shows when you will look at your price and availability again. If you want to hold dates for the client, tie them to a step such as the deposit and say so in the deposit wording.

faq.q: Does my cancellation clause replace a customer's cooling-off period?
faq.a: No. Citizens Advice calls 14 days the absolute minimum cooling-off period a seller must give for building or decorating work arranged by phone, online or away from the trader's premises, in England. Inside that period the customer can cancel and get all their money back if you have not started the work. Give a home customer in England written details of how to cancel with the quote, and let your own cancellation charges apply only after the 14 days.

faq.q: Which clauses should I leave out of a quote?
faq.a: Leave out a cap on liability, indemnity, ownership of designs, governing law and late-payment interest. Those belong in a written contract, and a lawyer is the right person to draft one.

Valid until the date shown at the top of this quote. After that date the price may change, and we will recheck it before you accept.
Not included: new bathroom fittings, floor tiling, plumbing or electrical work, and painting the ceiling. Anything not listed in this quote is not included in the price.
The price assumes: access from 8:00 to 17:00 on weekdays, power and water on, and walls that need only light patching. The tile allowance is £36 per m², so dearer tiles change the price.
Payment: a deposit of £520.00 including VAT is due when you accept. It books the start date and pays for the materials. The balance of £993.20 is due within 7 days of our invoice, which we send when the job is finished. Pay by bank transfer.
Changes: extra work, or a change to the tiles or the area, is priced and agreed with you in writing before we do it. If we find a hidden problem behind the old tiles, we will stop that part of the work, tell you and send a price for the repair.
Cooling-off period: you have 14 days to cancel this work, starting the day after you give the go-ahead. If you cancel in that time and we have not started the work, you get all your money back. If you ask us to start the work inside the 14 days and then cancel, you pay a part of the agreed price for the work done by then. To cancel, email us at the address on this quote.
Cancellation: after the cooling-off period, you can cancel before work starts by telling us in writing. If we have ordered materials we cannot return, you pay for them. If we have spent time on your job, you pay for that time at £23 an hour. We refund the rest of your deposit. This does not affect your legal rights.
Prices exclude VAT. VAT at 20% is shown in the totals above and the total includes VAT.
